section: Understanding Reparenting > Five Stages of Reparenting
before: Forced adulthood: You’re still stuck identifying as the lost inner child, forced frequently into handling situations that require more maturity, even if it looks like you’ve got it all together. At this stage, use your childlike superpowers to come into the “Wow of Now” (have you seen the movie Waking Life?), and make sure there’s enough safety around you to continue with reparenting. Begin to borrow adulthood--remember watching Mr. Rogers or Sesame Street? Those adult role models are what we’re looking for at this stage. This can almost feel like playing house as a kid where you imagined how you’d take care of a baby, etc. Practice being the adult--do at least one part of caring for yourself while support is still there from the previous step. Adult mode itself--after sufficient practice with reparenting, you become a natural at sending love to little you, protecting them, and shepherding them. Adult and child in relationship--the adult leads. The child isn’t pushed away, but doesn’t have to run the whole life alone. This can actually feel really weird if you’ve been stuck in forced adulthood for a while. Our goal is to go from weird to silly and playful. Lose self-consciousness while gaining self-awareness, if that makes sense!

section: Building Your Inner Adult > The Inner Guide: Becoming Your Own Shepherd > A Healthy Mind Is Not a Perfect Mind
before: I think this is closer to Buddhist practice too. The point is not an impossible performance in which nothing unskillful ever appears. In one discourse (sutta), AN 6.63, the Buddha defines karma in terms of intention (so if you didn’t mean to cause harm, your mind is not poisoned). In DN 2, he explains that in the training to purify the mind, one first recognizes a fault, makes amends, and then restrains themself to prevent that kind of thing in future. So it’s not like, “you’re either pure, or you’re not,” which is where a lot of folks stay stuck. If you’re ashamed about some pattern you have, that might be a signal to give some attention to how you can improve on that pattern. If it’s shame just because of an intrusive thought, then it’s probably not adaptive, and can be simply let go of.

before: Part of building who you are is untangling yourself from what I call the “belonging bargains” which pull you away from your own inner-knowing in return for belonging. A political tribe might expect consistent positions and predictable reactions, while a family or religion that’s kind to you might have expectations that look at face value like just being a good member. It can help to write down the unspoken rules your family ran on, like “Boys don’t cry.” Then write down the role you got handed, like the stand-in parent for a sibling, or the one who got blamed for everything (ST-CA has lists of both, in sections 15.2.3 and 15.2.4).

section: Conclusion and Appendix > Appendix > Schema Therapy
before: Of the scientifically studied clinical approaches I know, Schema Therapy, developed in the 1980s-1990s by Jeffrey E. Young, is the closest to this guide. Its therapists do what they call limited reparenting: within professional limits, they give you some of what a good parent would, with warmth and firmness and some playfulness too. Over time you take that in, and it becomes your own “Healthy Adult,” who looks after your “Vulnerable Child” and stands up to the punishing parent in your head. The healthy adult recognizes when a need differs from the strategy you use to meet it, and it helps you set limits. And it gets on with adult life, like work and the things you’ve committed to. All that sounds like my Nurturer, Protector and Guide by other names, and since the therapist’s version becomes yours bit by bit, it’s borrowed adulthood too.
